idiom_name: class with private-set properties and init/require validation
implementation_notes: Kotlin carries the classic structure with a regular class: private properties, init blocks and constructor require(...) checks establish the invariants, mutations go through intent-named methods, and private set publishes state read-only. Prefer a regular class for identity-bearing entities - data class generates equals, hashCode and copy that contradict identity - and use @JvmInline value class for typed ids and small value objects (zero-cost wrappers) plus immutable data classes for values. The classic form stays justified for anything with a lifecycle.
pitfalls: A data class generates a public copy() (and componentN) that can create invalid instances; annotate with @ConsistentCopyVisibility (Kotlin 2.0+) or keep entities as regular classes.
private set protects the write but the getter still exposes the state; return copies or read-only views for collections.
Value classes are inlined wrappers with no identity - never model an entity as a value class.

variants.name: Validated immutable data class with a private constructor
variants.implementation_notes: The model is immutable: a data class with a private primary constructor and val-only state, where every creation goes through a companion factory that validates and returns Either<DomainError, T> (Arrow) instead of throwing. State changes produce a new instance through domain methods or the companion, so an invariant cannot be broken by in-place mutation, and the generated copy() is constrained to the constructor's visibility. Choose it when the domain is value-oriented or the team prefers explicit error types; the cost is one allocation per transition and extra ceremony for identity-heavy aggregates.
pitfalls: The generated copy() honours the constructor visibility from Kotlin 2.0 (@ConsistentCopyVisibility); on older versions it could act as a public back door around the private constructor.
A data class gives structural equality: override equals/hashCode by id for identity-bearing concepts, or keep those as regular classes.
Either is contagious - convert to exceptions at the application boundary if the rest of the codebase is exception-based.
